items.body:
Pianist Kenny Barron (b. 1943) has paid his dues, working in the bands of Yusef Lateef and Dizzy Gillespie as well as a three-year stint in trumpeter Freddie Hubbard 's band. His work as a leader has also soared. His first album under his own name was titled You Had Better Listen (Atlantic, 1967). That title offered good advice. As with most top-tier jazz artists who boast 50-plus-year careers, he has played thousands of concerts, and many of these have surely been recorded, only to be forgotten, the tapes shelved. So Zev Feldman —who so often finds and produces for release lost recordings from jazz giants past and present (saxophonist Joe Henderson , pianists Cecil Taylor , Ahmad Jamal , Mal Waldron and Bill Evans , multiple-reedman Yusef Lateef )—offers up a superb trio outing from Barron: So Many Lovely Things: Live In Brecon . The 2-disc set was recorded in 1995 at the Brecon Jazz Festival in Wales with his then-current trio—Ray Drummond on bass and drummer Bill Riley. The music sparkles for the duration of it 100-plus minutes.  Barron's sound has always had a classy sheen, in the manner of Hank Jones and Tommy Flanagan , or—to bring it up to a current player— Bill Cunliffe . Opening with "Oh, Look At Me Now, a 1940 Frank Sinatra vehicle written by Joe Bushkin, the trio's brio and ebullience is on full display. They sound playful and full of the joy of creation as they stretch out the tune to 11 minutes of 'let's see what happens' charm. This is followed up by trumpeter Freddie Hubbard 's "Up Jumped Spring," which sounds majestic and lighthearted before Barron strides into Thelonious Monk 's "Shuffle Boil. Most of the tunes here are extended pieces, the familiar—Ray Noble's  "The Very Thought of You," "Ask Me Now" (another Monk gem) and "The Surrey With The Fringe On Top"—stretched out while maintaining the threads of their original melodies. This is Barron, 30 years into a stellar career, playing at the top of his considerable power, accompanied by an exceptional trio. Barron's previously mentioned first recording was aptly titled, so is So Many Lovely Things .

CD 1: Oh, Look At Me Now; Up Jumped Spring; Shuffle Boil; Time Was; Silent Rain; Ask Me Now.
CD 2: Nikara's Song; The Surrey with the Fringe on Top; The Very Thought of You; Canadian Sunset.

Personnel: Kenny Barron piano Ray Drummond bass, acoustic Ben Riley drums

items.body:
In a true meeting of great minds, shared aesthetic, and Nonesuch label mates, trumpeter/composer Ambrose Akinmusire and guitarist/composer Mary Halvorson play intently with their new Halvorson and hand-me-down Akinmusire Line 6 DL4 MkII Delay Modeler, and break the dark silence with the spectral movement of Slo-Mo Neon Luminate Hoverings . More laid back and ambient than either of the influencers' past works—Halvorson's 2022 Nonesuch debut Amaryllis and Belladonna ; Code Girl (Nonesuch, 2024); or Akinmusire's Grammy-nominated On the Tender Spot of Every Calloused Moment (Blue Note, 2020) and Origami Harvest (Blue Note, 2018) — Slo-Mo Neon Luminate Hoverings ruminates as it illuminates. "Prelude In the Ash" sets things in motion with the trumpeter's one-man-standing-in-the-morning declamation. Halvorson drifts in with a simple circular pattern, one that grows and bends as it evolves. And though "Prelude In the Ash" may not be the kind of world-beater one might expect from this music of giants, it sets the tone. Only to have track two, "This Vivid," obliterate the set tone. Arriving with a literal scream that loops back on itself and its audience as the duo have their way with time and space and other abstract thoughts. If you think about the alternate soundtrack for an average hour in post-America, who better than Akinmusire and Halvorson to give us one? The Morse code-ish, "Nice to meet you again for the first time," sets sail as a baleful conversation between equals ensues. With all its errant squiggles and sharp turns, "Soundcheck" hypnotizes as it unravels like an ancient mystery: clouds part, fog sets in. Halvorson's innate humor is fully focused as she adroitly sculpts her sound at will, creating a dream environment for  Akinmusire to float and revel in. Set in the diaspora at the end of the world, "Tangled Pretty" is another of those lost alternate soundtracks about a place in time. A place in the mind. A place where thought and moment happen. And what happens is a joining of hearts: Akinmusire calling to a higher realm as Halvorson paints the walls of said realm. Featuring Akinmusire's first use of delay and his interaction with and against the evolving sound, Slo-Mo Neon Luminate Hoverings continues tidally with "Ofo," an off-the-cuff rendering of the day that was. The reflective "Blood and Sand" and the sonically cinematic title track bring the set to a soaring close. Unfortunately, that is where the joyful hypnosis ends and the exhausting day begins.

Personnel: Mary Halvorson guitar Ambrose Akinmusire trumpet

Title: Slo-Mo Neon Luminate Hoverings | Year Released: 2027                    
                    						| Record Label: Self Produced

items.body:
Accomplished flutist Ali Ryerson is one of the most exciting proponents of the instrument in jazz. Over the course of a long career, both performing and teaching, she has honed a unique style. It is rooted in the Western classical tradition.  Yet it has a boppish and soulful spontaneity.  Her 17th release as a leader, simply titled The Ali Ryerson Quartet, showcases her masterful command of the instrument and signature sound. The energetic "Chuck's Tune" is a perfect introduction to this effervescent album. After the band plays the main theme, each member takes a brief solo, setting the stage for Ryerson's intricately constructed improvisation. The flutist's agile lines flitter through the laid-back cadence, creating an impressionistic melody.  Pianist Larry Ham takes center stage with a bluesy embellishment of the main theme. Bassist Lou Pappas follows with lyricism and elegance.  Drummer Tom Melito 's suave solo is punctuated by brief refrains from his bandmates, resulting in a delightful repartee. This type of camaraderie marks the entire recording, giving it a dynamic structure. For instance, on the energetic "Before Today." Pappas tastefully interprets the main theme and exchanges vibrant phrases with Ryerson before the leader launches into a warm and captivating performance.  Ham's response, as he takes his place in the spotlight, is mellifluous and polished.  Ryerson then leads the ensemble in a lively collective discourse that ushers in the tune's exciting conclusion. Ryerson tackles Brazilian bossa nova with the same sophisticated musicianship as American blues. The infectious groove of "Nada Como Ter Amor" that the side men create buoys Ryerson's resonant flute.  Ryerson's well-structured extemporization, nevertheless, crackles with spontaneity and reserved passion.  Ham adds a touch of romance to the song with his cascading notes, especially as he engages the leader in a graceful duet. The swinging "AliCat Blues," meanwhile, opens with Ham's crisp chords.  The rhythm trio's vamps simmer with soul, perfectly complementing Ryerson's cool, haunting musings. On this captivating set, Ryerson demonstrates her mature creativity and undampened, youthful enthusiasm. Ryerson and her side men craft music that is accessible without being humdrum and stimulating without being self-indulgent. The result is a charming and cohesive work that makes for a satisfying listen and should have a wide appeal.

Personnel: Ali Ryerson flute Larry Ham piano Lou Pappas bass Tom Melito drums

items.body:
The release of Crazy World of Love marks a new chapter for Louise Alexandra, a jazz vocalist whose artistry is as deep as her background is unconventional. Splitting her time between the vanguard of medical science and the timeless traditions of jazz, Alexandra is a Dutch-American vocalist, songwriter, and active cancer research scientist. For over 15 years, she built a formidable reputation within Boston's highly competitive biotech and jazz circuits before returning to the Netherlands, where she continues to develop cancer therapies while pursuing her musical evolution with enhanced focus. Alexandra's former name was Louise van Aarsen (that would be, Dr. Louise van Aarsen) before she sharpened her professional image as a singer. As a scientist, Alexandra concentrates on drug discovery, inflammation, vaccines, immunoassays, and genomics. She has successfully straddled the left-brain and right-brain worlds of science and music. Central to Alexandra's vocal identity is her profound association with the late Rebecca Parris , widely revered as Boston's "First Lady of Jazz" and a peer to legends like Sarah Vaughan and Carmen McRae . As Parris' student and trusted protégé, Alexandra absorbed the master's lessons in emotional delivery, phrasing, and stagecraft. Parris didn't just teach Alexandra; she actively mentored her career, directing and shaping her earliest recorded statements. Crazy World of Love stands on the shoulders of two previous, critically-respected studio albums that highlight Alexandra's steady artistic trajectory: the Parris-directed Destiny (Self Produced, 2012), recorded with premier Boston jazz musicians, established her clean, traditional sensibilities and sophisticated tone grownup music for grownups. Also directed by Parris was the follow-up recording, Today (Self Produced, 2020). This release revealed an increased confidence, deeper emotional nuance, and an expanding repertoire. While her previous catalog firmly rooted her in the rich tradition of the New England jazz scene, Crazy World of Love represents a major geographical and stylistic leap. Collaborating with Dutch jazz royalty—including pianist Rob van Bavel and his trio—Alexandra steps fully into her own as a lyricist and arranger, seamlessly bridging her American jazz upbringing with a vibrant European sensibility. The recording has several highlights, including Emmett Cohen Trio 's "Angel of Mine," to which Alexandra penned lyrics she shared with Benny Bernack III , who also played flugelhorn on the song. The singer breaks out her impressive vocalese chops on "East of the Sun," "Crazy World of Love," and "Hershey Bar / Little Did I Dream." The singer gets personal on the ballad "We Had It All." Alexandra paints a very adult picture of growing together and apart sans any romantic affect. She tells it like it is. The spirit of Parris, always close, becomes tactile on the "Some Other Time / We'll Be Together Again" diptych. Alexandra creates a panorama of love in all its guises on Crazy World of Love .

Personnel: Louise Alexandra vocals Rob van Bavel piano Frans van Geest bass, acoustic Marcel Serierse drums Vincent Koning guitar Jan Menu saxophone Benny Benack III trumpet and vocals
